claim: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the most common cause of inherited intellectual disability.
source: Loss of the RNA binding protein FMRP causes Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), the most common cause of inherited intellectual disability, yet it is unknown how FMRP function varies across brain regions and cell types and how this contributes to disease pathophysiology.
evidence: This is stated as established fact in the abstract and introduction, representing accepted scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of FMRP causes Fragile X Syndrome.

evidence: This is stated as established fact and represents well-established scientific knowledge about the cause of FXS.

claim: FMRP function varies across brain regions and cell types in ways that are currently unknown.

claim: FMRP binds autism-relevant mRNAs in a CA1-enriched manner.
source: Integrating these data with analysis of ribosome-bound transcripts in these neurons revealed CA1-enriched binding of autism-relevant mRNAs, and CA1-specific regulation of transcripts encoding circadian proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of CLIP and TRAP data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3.

claim: FMRP regulates transcripts encoding circadian proteins in a CA1-specific manner.
source: Integrating these data with analysis of ribosome-bound transcripts in these neurons revealed CA1-enriched binding of autism-relevant mRNAs, and CA1-specific regulation of transcripts encoding circadian proteins.
evidence: This is supported by CLIP and TRAP data showing differential regulation in CA1 versus cerebellar granule neurons, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: FMRP targets differ between CA1 pyramidal neurons and cerebellar granule neurons.
source: This contrasted with different targets in cerebellar granule neurons, and was consistent with circadian defects in hippocampus-dependent memory in Fmr1 knockout mice.
evidence: This is supported by comparative CLIP analysis between the two cell types as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fmr1 knockout mice exhibit circadian defects in hippocampus-dependent memory.
source: This contrasted with different targets in cerebellar granule neurons, and was consistent with circadian defects in hippocampus-dependent memory in Fmr1 knockout mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from object location memory and contextual fear conditioning tasks performed at different times of day, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Differential FMRP-dependent regulation of mRNAs across neuronal cell types may contribute to memory defects associated with FXS.
source: These findings demonstrate differential FMRP-dependent regulation of mRNAs across neuronal cell types that may contribute to phenotypes such as memory defects and sleep disturbance associated with FXS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined CLIP, TRAP, and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differential FMRP-dependent regulation of mRNAs across neuronal cell types may contribute to sleep disturbance associated with FXS.
source: These findings demonstrate differential FMRP-dependent regulation of mRNAs across neuronal cell types that may contribute to phenotypes such as memory defects and sleep disturbance associated with FXS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that FMRP regulates circadian transcripts in CA1 neurons.

claim: FXS is the leading monogenic cause of autism.
source: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and leading monogenic cause of autism, results from loss of function of the RNA binding protein FMRP (Hagerman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation to Hagerman et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of FMRP function is typically due to transcriptional silencing of the Fmr1 gene.
source: This loss of function is typically due to transcriptional silencing of the Fmr1 gene (Pieretti et al., 1991), although missense mutations in either of the KH-type RNA binding domains, frame shift mutations and deletions can also cause the phenotype in human (Coffee et al., 2008; De Boulle et al., 1993; Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2015; Hammond et al., 1997; Lugenbeel et al., 1995; Myrick et al., 2014; Quartier et al., 2017; Sitzmann et al., 2018; Suhl and Warren, 2015) and rodent models (Till et al., 2015; Zang et al., 2009).

claim: Fmr1 knockout mice exhibit defects in neuronal circuits involved in hippocampal memory.
source: The Fmr1 knockout (KO) mouse, or Fmr1 knock-in mouse harboring a I304N missense mutation (Zang et al., 2009) seen in a severely affected FXS individual (De Boulle et al., 1993), exhibit a range of neurologic, behavioral and cognitive deficits, including defects in neuronal circuits involved in hippocampal memory (Arbab et al., 2018; Boone et al., 2018; Huber et al., 2002; Talbot et al., 2018) and in circadian rhythm (Zhang et al., 2008), as well as altered dendritic spine morphology and dynamics, synaptic plasticity and neuronal circuits that model findings made in humans (Kazdoba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: cTag CLIP combines CLIP technology with the specificity conferred by Cre-lox technology.
source: This method, termed cTag CLIP (Hwang et al., 2017; Saito et al., 2018; Ule et al., 2018), combines CLIP (UV cross-linking immunoprecipitation) technology with the specificity that can be conferred by Cre-lox technology.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology supported by citations.

claim: RNA binding proteins are modified by homologous recombination to allow Cre-dependent knock-ins of epitope tags in cTag CLIP.
source: RNA binding proteins are modified by homologous recombination to allow Cre-dependent knock-ins of epitope tags that are then used for CLIP purification.
evidence: This describes the technical approach of the cTag CLIP method.

claim: cTag CLIP allows for minimal perturbation of the stoichiometry and regulation of the RNA binding protein of interest.
source: This cell-type specific Cre-lox mediated switching of epitope tags allows for minimal perturbation of the stoichiometry and regulation of the RNA binding protein of interest, a key factor in ascertaining biologically relevant RNA-protein interactions in vivo.
evidence: This is a stated advantage of the cTag CLIP methodology.

evidence: This describes the mouse model generated for the study, supported by a citation.

claim: A knock-in strategy was employed to target the endogenous Fmr1 locus in order to maintain wild-type gene expression and regulation.

evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The addition of the AcGFP-tag enables capture of all major isoforms of FMRP with the exception of a small minority of nuclear isoforms with an alternative c-terminus resulting from exclusion of exon 14.

claim: Nearly identical CLIP results have been observed with AcGFP-tagged FMRP and endogenous FMRP in forebrain neurons.

evidence: This validation is supported by a reference to Figure 2 in Van Driesche et al., 2019.

claim: The Camk2a-Cre mouse line drives Cre recombinase expression in a subset of forebrain excitatory neurons.
source: To achieve CA1-restricted expression of GFP-tagged FMRP, we crossed Fmr1-cTag mice with the Camk2a-Cre mouse line in which the mouse Camk2a promoter drives Cre recombinase expression in a subset of forebrain excitatory neurons and, within the hippocampus, specifically in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Tsien et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tsien et al., 1996.

claim: The Camk2a-Cre mouse line drives Cre recombinase expression specifically in CA1 pyramidal neurons within the hippocampus.

claim: Immunofluorescence of hippocampal tissue from Camk2a-Cre+/-; Fmr1-cTag+/Y confirmed clear expression of GFP in CA1 pyramidal cells.

evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No detectable GFP expression was observed in the absence of Cre recombinase.

evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Within CA1 pyramidal cells, expression of AcGFP-tagged FMRP was highest in the cell soma with detectable expression in the proximal dendrites.

claim: The expression pattern of AcGFP-tagged FMRP is consistent with that observed for endogenous FMRP.

claim: FMRP is predominantly associated with polyribosomes in the brain.

claim: Markers for other cell types are depleted in TRAP immunoprecipitation relative to input lysate.

evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CLIP tag density within the coding region was significantly correlated with the abundance of the transcript as measured by TRAP.

evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B with statistical testing.

claim: 327 stringent FMRP targets were defined as transcripts with a CLIP score >2 in all three replicates.

evidence: This describes the classification scheme for FMRP targets based on CLIP score analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 246 transcripts are uniquely identified as FMRP targets in CA1 neurons compared to whole brain and cerebellar granule cells.

evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CLIP scores defined in CA1 and cerebellar granule cells were significantly correlated.

evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Binding affinity is broadly conserved between CA1 and cerebellar granule cells.

evidence: This is inferred from the significant correlation of CLIP scores between the two cell types.

claim: FMRP binding was highly enriched on autism candidate mRNAs in CA1 neurons.
source: To further explore the association of FMRP with autism-related mRNAs, we examined binding to the mRNAs encoded by SFARI autism candidate genes in CA1 neurons (Figure 3C). Strikingly, FMRP binding was highly enriched on autism candidate mRNAs and the amount of binding correlated with the strength of evidence supporting the classification.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SFARI genes shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The amount of FMRP binding to autism candidate mRNAs correlated with the strength of evidence supporting their classification as autism genes.
source: Strikingly, FMRP binding was highly enriched on autism candidate mRNAs and the amount of binding correlated with the strength of evidence supporting the classification. That is to say that the higher the probability of a gene being causative to ASD phenotypes, the more highly bound it is by FMRP in CA1 neurons (Figure 3C; Wilcoxon rank sum test for SFARI gene clip scores compared to clip scores for all CA1 genes: SFARI category 1, p=8.1×10–11, n = 25; SFARI category 2, p=5.2×10–13, n = 61, SFARI category 3, p=2.3×10–16, n = 184; SFARI category 4, p<2.2×10–16, n = 437; SFARI category 5, p=3.5×10–4, n = 170; SFARI category 6, p=0.71, n = 24; SFARI Syndromic, p<2.2×10–16, n = 166).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FMRP binding is highly enriched on long transcripts in CA1 neurons.
source: To determine whether FMRP binding is enriched on long transcripts in CA1 neurons, we examined the length of transcripts in our subclasses of targets. FMRP binding is highly enriched on long transcripts (length of FMRP targets vs CA1 expressed transcripts, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<2.2×10–6) and transcript length increases for more highly bound targets (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3E with statistical testing.

claim: Transcript length increases for more highly bound FMRP targets.
source: FMRP binding is highly enriched on long transcripts (length of FMRP targets vs CA1 expressed transcripts, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<2.2×10–6) and transcript length increases for more highly bound targets (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A significant overlap was observed between FMRP and MeCP2 targets.
source: Given the existing evidence that mutations in MeCP2, the underlying cause of Rett Syndrome, may cause neurological dysfunction by specifically disrupting long gene expression in the brain, and previously reported overlaps between FMRP and MeCP2 targets, we tested the overlap of our CA1 FMRP target list with a set of genes that are transcriptionally repressed by MeCP2 (Gabel et al., 2015). A significant overlap was observed between FMRP and MeCP2 targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Fishers exact test, p=6.94×10−6) and MeCP2 targets were found to have a small but significant decrease in TRAP from Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<2.2×10−16).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MeCP2 targets were found to have a small but significant decrease in TRAP from Fmr1 KO mice.
source: A significant overlap was observed between FMRP and MeCP2 targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Fishers exact test, p=6.94×10−6) and MeCP2 targets were found to have a small but significant decrease in TRAP from Fmr1 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<2.2×10−16).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only a minority of MeCP2-repressed genes are FMRP targets.
source: However, only a minority of MeCP2-repressed genes are FMRP targets, with 20.7% having a CLIP score >1 and 5.3% being classed as stringent FMRP targets.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the overlap analysis.

claim: Length-matched transcripts with low or no FMRP binding showed no dysregulation in the Fmr1 KO.
source: To further explore the link between FMRP binding and transcript length, we compared FMRP targets to a random set of length-matched transcripts with either low or no FMRP binding. The length-matched set of transcripts showed no dysregulation in the Fmr1 KO (Figure 3F), suggesting that length is not the sole determining factor in FMRP binding and that there is specificity of binding and regulation even among a long cohort of transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3F.

evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gene sets related to circadian gene expression were significantly enriched among FMRP targets.
source: To more broadly assess the biological function of FMRP in CA1 using a diverse set of literature-curated gene sets, we performed Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on our CLIP score ranked list and Fmr1 KO TRAP fold change ranked list (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). This is a computational method that determines whether an a priori defined set of genes shows statistically significant, concordant differences between two biological states (e.g. bound vs unbound by CLIP or down-regulated vs up-regulated by TRAP) (Mootha et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005). The algorithm takes a user supplied ranked list of genes and performs an unbiased search for gene sets that are statistically enriched at either end of the ranked list. Strikingly, gene sets related to circadian gene expression were significantly enriched among FMRP targets and were down-regulated in Fmr1 KO.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the suprachiasmatic nucleus, Fxr2 was found to have a greater effect on circadian gene expression than Fmr1.
source: However, in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the central brain region for regulation of circadian rhythm, Fxr2 was found to have a greater effect on circadian gene expression, with significant differences in the expression of core circadian genes observed only in Fxr2 KO and Fmr1/Fxr2 double KO mice but not Fmr1 KO mice (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: The hippocampus is a convergence point of sleep and memory.
source: In particular, the hippocampus is a convergence point of sleep and memory.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Clock genes are expressed rhythmically in the hippocampus in mice and humans.
source: Clock genes are expressed rhythmically in the hippocampus in mice and humans (Jilg et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2016) and hippocampal slices continue these oscillations in culture indicating an intrinsic circadian expression independent of the SCN (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Hippocampal slices continue circadian oscillations in culture indicating an intrinsic circadian expression independent of the SCN.
source: Clock genes are expressed rhythmically in the hippocampus in mice and humans (Jilg et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2016) and hippocampal slices continue these oscillations in culture indicating an intrinsic circadian expression independent of the SCN (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2009.

claim: Circadian rhythms have been shown in hippocampal long term potentiation at CA1 synapses.
source: Circadian rhythms have also been shown in hippocampal long term potentiation at CA1 synapses (Chaudhury et al., 2005), in firing rates of CA1 place cells (Munn and Bilkey, 2012) and in memory acquisition and recall (Smarr et al., 2014; Snider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaudhury et al., 2005.

claim: Circadian rhythms have been shown in firing rates of CA1 place cells.
source: Circadian rhythms have also been shown in hippocampal long term potentiation at CA1 synapses (Chaudhury et al., 2005), in firing rates of CA1 place cells (Munn and Bilkey, 2012) and in memory acquisition and recall (Smarr et al., 2014; Snider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Munn and Bilkey, 2012.

claim: Circadian rhythms have been shown in memory acquisition and recall.
source: Circadian rhythms have also been shown in hippocampal long term potentiation at CA1 synapses (Chaudhury et al., 2005), in firing rates of CA1 place cells (Munn and Bilkey, 2012) and in memory acquisition and recall (Smarr et al., 2014; Snider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smarr et al., 2014 and Snider et al., 2018.

claim: Deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning tasks have been observed in mice following disruption of key circadian genes including Per1, Cry1/2, Clock and Arnt (Bmal1).
source: Deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning tasks have previously been observed in mice following disruption of key circadian genes including Per1, Cry1/2, Clock and Arnt (Bmal1l) (Jilg et al., 2010; Sei et al., 2006; Snider and Obrietan, 2018; Van der Zee et al., 2008; Wardlaw et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Conditional deletion of Bmal1 in forebrain excitatory neurons but not in the SCN causes deficits in Barnes maze performance and novel object location and novel object recognition tasks in the absence of any change in circadian locomotor activity.
source: Moreover, conditional deletion of Bmal1 in forebrain excitatory neurons but not in the SCN, using Camk2a-Cre, causes deficits in Barnes maze performance and novel object location and novel object recognition tasks in the absence of any change in circadian locomotor activity (Snider et al., 2016; Snider and Obrietan, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Snider et al., 2016 and Snider and Obrietan, 2018.

claim: These findings support a direct role for clock gene expression outside of the SCN in hippocampal function.
source: These findings support a direct role for clock gene expression outside of the SCN in hippocampal function and demonstrate that circadian rhythms in learning and memory can be independent of locomotor rhythms.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that hippocampal-specific manipulations affect memory without affecting locomotor rhythms.

claim: Circadian rhythms in learning and memory can be independent of locomotor rhythms.
source: These findings support a direct role for clock gene expression outside of the SCN in hippocampal function and demonstrate that circadian rhythms in learning and memory can be independent of locomotor rhythms.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that hippocampal-specific manipulations affect memory without affecting locomotor rhythms.

claim: The data indicate for the first time a direct role for FMRP in the regulation of transcripts critical for circadian function in the hippocampus.
source: Our data indicate for the first time a direct role for FMRP in the regulation of transcripts critical for circadian function in the hippocampus and allow us to establish a molecular correlate of circadian defect in excitatory neurons in the brain.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the novel findings from the study.

claim: The data allow establishment of a molecular correlate of circadian defect in excitatory neurons in the brain.
source: Our data indicate for the first time a direct role for FMRP in the regulation of transcripts critical for circadian function in the hippocampus and allow us to establish a molecular correlate of circadian defect in excitatory neurons in the brain.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the novel findings from the study.

claim: There is specific regulation of circadian transcripts in CA1 pyramidal cells but not cerebellar granule cells.
source: We find a specific regulation of circadian transcripts in CA1 pyramidal cells but not cerebellar granule cells, despite similar expression of these transcripts in both cell types (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The finding of cell-type specific circadian control is an important new observation.
source: Nonetheless, the finding of cell-type specific circadian control in general, and additionally that such regulation can be FMRP-dependent, are important new observations.
evidence: This is a statement of the significance of the findings.

claim: Circadian control can be FMRP-dependent.
source: Nonetheless, the finding of cell-type specific circadian control in general, and additionally that such regulation can be FMRP-dependent, are important new observations.
evidence: This is a statement of the significance of the findings.

claim: Aberrant regulation of circadian transcripts in CA1 neurons suggested the possibility of a circadian defect in memory in the absence of FMRP.
source: Given the nature of the functions attributed to CA1 neurons, aberrant regulation of circadian transcripts in this cell type suggested the possibility of a circadian defect in memory in the absence of FMRP.
evidence: This is an inference that motivated the behavioral experiments.

claim: The absence of FMRP in humans and in animal models is well-established to cause memory defects.
source: While the absence of FMRP in humans (Schmitt et al., 2019) and in animal models (Drozd et al., 2018; Kazdoba et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2017; Till et al., 2015) is well-established to cause memory defects, our studies are able to extend these observations by demonstrating that defects in at least two modes of learning and memory are dependent on the phase of the circadian cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Defects in at least two modes of learning and memory in Fmr1 KO mice are dependent on the phase of the circadian cycle.
source: While the absence of FMRP in humans (Schmitt et al., 2019) and in animal models (Drozd et al., 2018; Kazdoba et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2017; Till et al., 2015) is well-established to cause memory defects, our studies are able to extend these observations by demonstrating that defects in at least two modes of learning and memory are dependent on the phase of the circadian cycle.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data from object location memory and contextual fear conditioning.

claim: Fmr1 KO mice show deficits in object location memory but not contextual fear conditioning during the day, which is consistent with findings of others.
source: Our findings that Fmr1 KO mice show deficits in object location memory but not contextual fear conditioning during the day, is consistent with findings of others (Dobkin et al., 2000; King and Jope, 2013; Peier et al., 2000; Van Dam et al., 2000) but reveal an unexpected dependence of these findings on the phase of the circadian cycle in which they are tested.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The behavioral findings reveal an unexpected dependence on the phase of the circadian cycle in which they are tested.
source: Our findings that Fmr1 KO mice show deficits in object location memory but not contextual fear conditioning during the day, is consistent with findings of others (Dobkin et al., 2000; King and Jope, 2013; Peier et al., 2000; Van Dam et al., 2000) but reveal an unexpected dependence of these findings on the phase of the circadian cycle in which they are tested.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the current study.

claim: Circadian differences are not observed in other behavioral characteristics that are less dependent on the hippocampus, including hyperactivity and anxiety.
source: Moreover, consistent with our findings that circadian transcripts are specifically regulated by FMRP in the CA1, circadian differences are not observed in other behavioral characteristics that are less dependent on the hippocampus, including hyperactivity (Figure 5B, Saré et al., 2016) and anxiety (Saré et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data and a citation to Saré et al., 2016.

claim: Memory consolidation, including spatial memory encoded by hippocampal place cells, is believed to occur during sleep.
source: Memory consolidation, including spatial memory encoded by hippocampal place cells, is believed to occur during sleep (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) and FMRP has been shown to play an important role in sleep-dependent synaptic homeostasis in Drosophila (Bushey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FMRP has been shown to play an important role in sleep-dependent synaptic homeostasis in Drosophila.
source: Memory consolidation, including spatial memory encoded by hippocampal place cells, is believed to occur during sleep (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) and FMRP has been shown to play an important role in sleep-dependent synaptic homeostasis in Drosophila (Bushey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bushey et al., 2011.

claim: The deficits observed in spatial and contextual memory may be the result of sleep disturbance or an independent function of the circadian genes in learning and memory within the hippocampus.
source: Thus, the deficits observed in spatial and contextual memory may be the result of sleep disturbance or an independent function of the circadian genes in learning and memory within the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: The results combined with previous findings of others are suggestive of a direct link between altered circadian gene expression in the hippocampal CA1 region and altered CA1-dependent circadian behaviors.
source: While our results combined with previous findings of others are suggestive of a direct link between altered circadian gene expression in the hippocampal CA1 region and altered CA1-dependent circadian behaviors, it remains to be tested whether other cell types or brain regions also contribute to these phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined molecular and behavioral data.

claim: It remains to be tested whether other cell types or brain regions also contribute to the circadian memory phenotypes.
source: While our results combined with previous findings of others are suggestive of a direct link between altered circadian gene expression in the hippocampal CA1 region and altered CA1-dependent circadian behaviors, it remains to be tested whether other cell types or brain regions also contribute to these phenotypes.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction for research.

claim: Altered circadian brain rhythms may contribute to the deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning and memory in FXS.
source: Together our findings indicate that altered circadian brain rhythms may contribute to the deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning and memory in FXS.
evidence: This is a concluding inference based on the combined findings of the study.
